item.title: Where Do You Stand on the Seven Deadly Sins and Virtues?
item.description:
Personality

Where Do You Stand on the Seven Deadly Sins and Virtues?

Test yourself on these time-honored approaches to goodness and evil.

Posted October 3, 2026

Key points
  • Sins and virtues are thought of in religious terms, but they can translate into psychology.
  • A new measure allows you to test your own tendencies to appeal to your better nature as you go through life.
  • By focusing on strengths rather than weaknesses, you can strive for the fulfillment that comes from virtue.

Theologians have long thought that our inner core has tendencies to sin and to do good. Psychologists instead talk about the dark triad, composed of narcissism, psychopathy, and Machiavellianism. These malevolent traits are balanced by the bright side of personality, focusing on happiness, optimism, and altruism. As in virtually all of the arts, fascination with the dark side in psychology outweighs attempts to define and measure the good in humanity. The question is whether personality can be mapped onto the tendency to sin or possess virtues.

Psychology Tackles Sins and Vices

In a new paper by Norwegian Business School’s Adrian Furman and colleagues (2026), a new self-rating questionnaire designed to improve existing measures addresses this question. Previously, the Vices and Virtues Scale tested vices only and used single-item ratings for each sin. By expanding the instrument to the positive qualities and combining self-ratings into longer scales, the authors believed their new approach would produce a more reliable instrument with two 7-item scales.

Conceptually, quantifying sins and virtues into a reliable measure also allows for these qualities to be compared to scores on standard personality instruments believed to relate to the tendency to be good versus the tendency to be bad. Here’s where the dark triad comes in with the added quality of sadism, making the cluster of qualities into the dark tetrad.

One qualification worth mentioning here is that personality psychologists are starting to complain that the dark triad-tetrad is too simplistic a notion to have validity. The terms themselves are too subjective, and the cluster may not always group into a neat three- or four-item bunch. Even so, each quality can be examined in relationship to sins and virtues.

Translating into lay terms, Machiavellianism becomes “crafty,” narcissism translates into “special,” psychopathy into “wild,” and sadism into “mean.” Theory would predict that each of these individually or as a group would relate to sinfulness and virtue.

Test Yourself: The Seven Sins and Virtues Questionnaire

In a pilot study, the authors tested the statistical structure of their new measure, called the “Self-Rated Sins and Virtues (SSRV)” scale. Here are the items which you can try rating yourself on a 0 to 100 scale:

Sins

Pride: conceit, immodesty, vainglory

Greed: avarice, covetousness, ravenous

Lust: inordinate, illicit sexual desire, appetitive

article continues after advertisement

Envy: jealousy, possessive, resentful

Gluttony: drunkenness, indulgent, excessive

Wrath: anger, irritation, annoyance

Sloth: laziness, idleness, energy-less

Virtues

Humility: modesty, humbleness, meekness

Charity: compassion, consideration, morality

Chastity: celibacy, self-restraint, control

Gratitude: gratefulness, thankfulness, recognition

Temperance: restraint, abstinence, moderation

Patience: tolerance, forbearance, self-control

Diligence: conscientiousness, industriousness, effortfulness

On average, of the 300 in the sample (average age 48), men scored 38 on sins and women scored 33. Everyone scored higher on virtues, with men at 55 and women at 59 (a significant difference).

The statistical case had strong support, and the 14 items fit into two 7-item scales. Additionally, people scoring high on psychopathy were more likely to admit to their sins and deny their virtues. The authors noted that, “It may be that psychopaths are indeed proud of this high sinfulness, not a virtuous profile” (p. 6).

The second study, using a similar demographic sample, tested how scores on these two scales would relate to theoretically related personality traits. The authors translated the dark tetrad questionnaire into another measure called “High Potential Trait Indicator (HPTI).” Expanding from the dark tetrad, the HPTI allows the assessment of conscientiousness, adjustment, curiosity, courage, ambiguity tolerance, and competitiveness. These validity-testing scales included ideology and self-esteem.

From these analyses, the authors concluded that their instrument did what it was supposed to statistically, and also related in expected ways to the HPTI. Overall, both studies showed that the highest self-rated sin was pride, and the highest virtue was gratitude. Optimistic people and older people in the sample were more likely to rate themselves as lower on sins than virtues.

People low in conscientiousness, adjustment, and courageousness rated themselves higher on sins and lower on virtues. Competitive people were more likely to admit to sinning, and curious people saw themselves as more virtuous. The authors noted that the competitiveness finding is interesting and makes sense; sinning may seem less sinful in someone who wants to get ahead. Beware of the competitive person, then, as it’s likely someone with few guardrails on cutting you off to gain advantages.

article continues after advertisement

Putting Your Sins and Virtues to the Test

The SSRV was quick to administer (less than three minutes); it provides a handy tool for giving yourself a morality check. Impression management and social desirability always lurk in the background in any self-report measure, but particularly one with such loaded terms as having “illicit sexual desires.” Furman and his colleagues were relatively skeptical of some of their findings, noting that how people rate themselves doesn’t always conform to how they behave. However, in your heart of hearts, with no one entering your ratings into a database, you can use this measure to translate your strengths and weaknesses potentially into qualities you can better balance in your future behavior.

To sum up, morality tends to be a little-used concept in psychology. By turning the perhaps vague ideas of sins and virtues into concrete self-ratings, you can gain the fulfillment that comes with seeing the light rather than the dark in yourself.

item.title: Affective Reactivity: A Transdiagnostic Risk Factor?
item.description:
Psychological Evaluation

Affective Reactivity: A Transdiagnostic Risk Factor?

Strong emotional reaction to either a win or loss may point to greater risk.

Posted October 3, 2026

Key points
  • The current categorical diagnostic system is problematic.
  • A dimensional approach may improve diagnostic accuracy and treatment efficacy.
  • Identifying transdiagnostic commonalities is an important step toward such improvement.
  • Emotional reactivity may be one such commonality.

It is now well accepted among psychologists and clinical researchers that the official categories we use to diagnose mental disorders, those familiar labels such as major depressive disorder, generalized anxiety disorder, etc., are inadequate in that they do not “carve nature at the joints.” In other words, our current categories are not discrete but highly overlapping, so that many disorders share diagnostic features and symptoms.

Moreover, treatment modalities are often effective across diagnostic labels. Medications, too, tend to work for multiple diagnoses. Our current categories, finally, are not based on biological or etiological similarities but on committee consensus regarding co-occurring symptoms and clinical courses.

This fact has given rise in recent decades to an alternative, dimensional approach, which involves a search for transdiagnostic commonalities, both at the level of treatment and coping (techniques that work for multiple psychological problems) and at the diagnostic level (i.e., vulnerabilities that predispose individuals to a vast array of potential dysfunctional manifestations). We know, for example, that cognitive restructuring, psychological flexibility, and experiential engagement (exposure) are transdiagnostic coping and treatment mechanisms, useful in the treatment of multiple mood and anxiety problems. On the vulnerabilities front, we have good evidence that factors such as personality neuroticism, negative attributional style, executive function deficits, and uncertainty intolerance, as well as environmental factors such as social isolation, childhood chaos, or parental history of mental disorder predispose individuals to a host of psychological disorders.

One such transdiagnostic factor is affective dysfunction. Indeed, disturbances in emotion regulation and expression mark a host of mental disorders. Yet, these emotional disruptions differ from one disorder to the next (down mood in depression; manic mood in bipolar disorder, etc.). Thus, it is not easy to discern which aspects of dysregulated emotions are indeed transdiagnostic, appearing across discrete diagnoses. The challenge of our clinical science is to identify empirically these elusive transdiagnostic patterns of affective disturbance.

Recent research (2026) by Australian researcher Ashleigh Fulton and colleagues has addressed itself to this challenge, providing evidence that the culprit (or at least one of them) is what is known as affective reactivity, a tendency, identified in the mid-'90s, to express heightened immediate emotional reactions to emotion-eliciting stimuli (both positive and negative).

The authors set up two experiments to explore the link between symptom severity and emotional reactivity. Participants were adults aged 18 to 65 from six different countries. The final sample sizes for Experiment 1 and Experiment 2 were 320 participants and 509 participants, respectively.

In the initial phase of each experiment, participants completed a demographic questionnaire and a series of self-report questionnaires assessing the severity of emotional-disorder symptoms, including anxiety, hypomania, and anhedonia.

In the second phase of each experiment, participants completed a decision-making task while periodically reporting on their affective state. The task required participants to choose between two cards, each awarding them a different number of points. Before choosing, participants could see the two possible outcomes that could occur for each card if chosen (−200, −100, 0, 100, or 200 points) and the respective probabilities of each outcome (25 percent, 50 percent, or 75 percent). Cards were presented in four blocks of 53 trials each. Every three to five trials throughout the task, participants were asked to report their current emotional valence.

After a card was chosen, participants were shown both the outcome of their choice and the outcome of the unchosen card, which allowed the researchers to measure participants’ affective reactivity to both the gain/loss outcome of their chosen card and whether the outcome of the unchosen card was better or worse.

The main results showed that participants displayed significant affective reactivity to both the outcomes of the chosen card and the difference between this outcome and the outcome of the unchosen card. Specifically, greater rewards were associated with more positive subsequent affect and greater losses were associated with more negative subsequent affect. The converse was true of the unchosen card, in which better outcomes for the unchosen card produced more negative subsequent affect and vice versa.

As expected, more-severe symptoms of depression, anxiety, and anhedonia were all associated with a more negative average emotional valence, indicating that participants with more severe emotional symptoms experienced more negative affect during the task.

Second, across both experiments, participants who reported more severe hypomania or anxiety symptoms tended to have more positive affective reactions to winning points and more negative reactions to losing. In other words, anxiety and hypomania symptoms positively correlated with affective reactivity.

These findings join previous work to suggest that affective reactivity may indeed be one important dimension of mental health, and that individuals who are high on affective reactivity may be more vulnerable to mental health difficulties. The researchers conclude: “Our results therefore suggest that heightened affective reactivity to reward is a trait-like individual difference that is associated with increased risk for multiple different forms of psychopathology, consistent with the transdiagnostic perspective on affect disturbance in psychological disorders."

item.title: Spiritual Therapy Approaches That Manage Worry and Anxiety
item.description:
Spirituality

Spiritual Therapy Approaches That Manage Worry and Anxiety

On psychotherapy, spirituality, and anxiety.

Posted October 3, 2026

Key points
  • Religion predates psychotherapy as a means of mitigating human anxiety.
  • Spirituality can be a powerful factor in learning to manage stress and anxiety.
  • Spiritual approaches to anxiety can complement psychotherapy.
Buddha
Source: By Pierre André Leclercq - Own work, Wikimedia Commons

This is Part 2 of a series of posts on anxiety. See Part 1 here.

Psychotherapy, often coupled today with psychopharmacology, is the traditional Western go-to for treatment of anxiety. Existential psychotherapy, for instance, asserts that we must learn to accept and tolerate our anxiety, losses, and ultimately, mortality, and that some anxiety is the inescapable cost of being free, conscious, mortal, and responsible for ourselves. But, from a philosophical or spiritual perspective, is this necessarily so?

Philosopher and theologian Alan Watts didn't buy it (1951). He wondered what we lose if we stopped caring so much. In Buddhism, for instance, suffering or dukkha (which certainly includes the experience of worrying and anxiety) is seen as the consequence of having too much desire, grasping, or attachment. Attachment to material things. Desire to have certain feelings or experiences, and not others. Expectations about how life, relationships, and people should be, and what our labor will bring. Psychologist Albert Ellis (1957) focused on identifying and eliminating these “shoulds” and "musts," or at least converting them to preferences, in his rational-emotive behavior therapy.

But what if we actually have nothing to lose? Because, in reality, we have nothing but our existence itself. All else is non-essential accoutrements or accessories. And what if our existence is itself illusory, nothing more than a dream? A very convincing hallucination? Or, in Hindu and Buddhist terms, mere maya or illusion? (The Zen teacher Chuang Tzu dreamed he was a butterfly. When he woke, he wondered, "Am I a man who dreamt about being a butterfly, or am I really a butterfly who now dreams about being a man?") What then is there really left to worry or be anxious about?

Reaching this radical conclusion does not mean we no longer care about others or the world; we choose to be less attached and more accepting. Being in the world but not being of it, as Jesus of Nazareth taught. Ultimately, less anxiously attached to our own continued existence. And, therefore, less fearful of our own inevitable demise. We would presumably be virtually liberated from anxiety and worry.

But such liberation is much easier said than done. For one thing, the survival instinct—I call it the immortality drive—is primitive and supremely powerful (2026). Traditional Western religions serve a similar purpose: spiritual faith in an omnipotent God and belief in life after death make life more meaningful, mitigate anxiety, and diminish worrying. Blind faith and trust in a benevolent and omniscient God, and relinquishing control to that omnipotent deity, eliminate any need to worry about what will happen. It's now in God's hands, not our own.

The concept of predestination is another method to preclude the need to feel anxious and worry—that everything is cosmically predetermined and planned for us in life, that free will is illusory, and that, therefore, it makes no difference what our decisions and choices are since the outcome is already set. Yet, when faith is blind, we can no longer see the part we play in determining our own destiny, nor the responsibility we bear for our actions, which can lead to feelings such as frustration, powerlessness, helplessness, victimhood, apathy, or grandiosity.

Still, there is no denying that anxiety, and especially death anxiety (see, for example, Becker, 1973)—or really, it's avoidance and denial—is the surreptitious source of so many of our daily worries. When we carefully examine our worries and anxieties and carry them out to their logical conclusions, death is often secretly lurking.

But what happens when we discover that there really is no security in life? Except for that sense of security that comes from within. A spiritual or psychological rather than existential security. We arrive at what Watts (1951) termed the "wisdom of insecurity." We see that our worrying was always a way of denying or trying to control these disturbing existential facts of life. Of avoiding rather than accepting existential anxiety.

Practicing Mindfulness

Relinquishing our illusions of control, accepting our relative powerlessness over life and death, and accepting ourselves as we are, including our anxiety, can be liberating. It allows us to stop worrying and get on with the daily business of living. The mysterious future will unfold for us soon enough. Make necessary plans and decisions. But don't dwell on them or their desired outcomes.

Here is a little parable that can, especially in anxious times, serve to exemplify and remind us of how to practice such mindful presence:

When a Zen monk's mindful walk in the woods is interrupted by a ravenous tiger ready to make a meal of him, the monk runs for his life with the tiger in hot pursuit. Weaving through the trees, he comes upon a clearing and suddenly stops: The monk finds himself teetering at the edge of a sheer cliff, hundreds of feet high, with only jagged rocks below. Still trying to evade the tiger's terrifying teeth and claws and with no other escape route, he slowly descends several feet down the steep precipice, precariously clinging to a tree root, hoping that the ravenous cat will eventually give up the chase. Meanwhile, the hungry tiger looms menacingly above him, snarling, salivating, pawing at his potential prey, and patiently waiting. At the same time, the slender root the monk desperately clings to starts to snap. Mindful of the dubious reality of his predicament, with certain death seemingly awaiting him above and below, the monk suddenly notices a gorgeous, juicy wild strawberry growing from the cliffside barely within his grasp. He is aware that his mouth is bone dry due to the anxiety of his imminent life-and-death situation and can feel the sweat trickling down from his forehead as well as the gentle ocean breeze cooling his brow and his own rhythmic breathing. He focuses intently upon and appreciates the strawberry's beautiful gem-like color, bright green leaves, and ripe, redolent, fruity fragrance. Plucking the strawberry with his one free hand, still clinging for dear life to the fragile tree root, the mindful monk puts it in his mouth and savors its tart, bittersweet taste and juicy succulence.

item.title: How Meet-Cute Has Become a Dating Trend Again
item.description:
Mating

How Meet-Cute Has Become a Dating Trend Again

A majority of relationships are starting IRL.

Posted October 3, 2026

Key points
  • A meet-cute is a fun, quirky, or accidental first meeting between two people who eventually fall in love.
  • Even with the rise of online dating, the majority of couples may still be meeting initially in real life.
  • The interest in meet-cutes seems to be growing, reflecting a desire for authenticity and IRL connections.
  • The meet-cute trend is a reminder to leave yourself open to different possibilities and serendipity.
Source: Gustavo Fring/Pexels

How did the two of you first meet? Well, remember that time when you were both at Bloomingdale's in New York City shopping for Christmas gifts for each of your partners at the time, and then both of you reached for the exact same pair of cashmere gloves at the exact same time? What were the chances of that happening?

Wait, maybe that wasn't your story. That was instead how Jonathan (played by John Cusack) and Sara (played by Kate Beckinsale) first met in the totally fictional 2001 romantic comedy movie Serendipity. Oh well, that would have been a cute way to first meet. You could even say that it was a meet-cute.

Meet-Cute Emerged From Rom-Coms

The "meet-cute" term first arose to describe such a scene in a rom-com where a couple first met because such scenes often are quite cute, especially when you know that they will end up together. It can even be awkward and contrary. One example was Harry's first meeting with Sally in the 1989 rom-com When Harry Met Sally—a drive from Chicago to New York City that had them bickering like cats and, well, cats that don't like each other. Another was Emily's heckling of Kumail during his comedy stand-up set in the 2017 movie The Big Sick.

Then there's the 2022 movie actually named Meet Cute, where Sheila uses a time machine to keep going back in time to try to create the perfect first meeting with Gary. The term has been around for so long, with origins tracing back to the 1930s, that it's already met the criteria to be in the Merriam-Webster dictionary. Nevertheless, the Meet Cute movie was quite "timely" in that it reflected a recent surge in interest in meet-cutes in real life, or IRL.

What Is a Meet-Cute

Yep, the term "meet-cute" can apply to real-life situations and relationships, too. It's when real-life couples have a "cute"—meaning accidental, quirky, or worth-telling-as-a-story—way that they first met. It's especially a meet-cute when chronicling the story can always elicit an "awwwww" or whatever sound you might make when you see a quokka or a sea otter in a bonnet.

One of the attractions to having a meet-cute story is the whole serendipity of that first encounter, which was the title of that movie in a deliberate, non-serendipitous way. The writers of the movie probably recognized the fact that a lot of people are enamored of the possibility of a long-term relationship or marriage being "meant to be." That a higher force like destiny wanted you to be together. Otherwise, why would the cosmos bring together two people seemingly randomly in such an odd and unexpected way?

Online Dating Seems to Have Reduced Meet-Cutes

At first glance, though, it seems like the rise of online dating has decreased the number of such meet-cutes. After all, people may not go "awwww" when they hear a story like, "Yeah, I swiped right" or "I messaged, 'I like your profile,' and the other person responded, 'Thanks. How you doing.'" Dating apps can bring an Amazon-esque, I-ordered-something-and-got-it type of transactional vibe to dating, quite different from a "we were meant to be" feeling.

For example, the other day I asked someone how she and her husband first met. She then kind of rolled her eyes and said, "Well, online, like, you know, everyone else." Not much of a cute story there.

Interest in Meet-Cute Appears to Be Growing

However, the "like everyone else" may not necessarily be the case. For example, a Hims survey found that 82 percent of 18- to 65-year-old men and women in relationships in the U.S. first met in person rather than online. Even though this percentage was lower among Gen Zers, it was still 77 percent for the 18- to 29-year-old age group. That means the vast majority of couples still might be having their own meet-cutes.

Plus, according to data from Eventbrite, there's been a 117 percent increase in events using meet-cute language being posted on the global events marketplace in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period from a year ago. Add to that the emergence of social media accounts like @meetcutesnyc, with 3.3M followers, to disseminate in real life (IRL) meet-cute stories, and it looks like more and more people are desiring to have meet-cutes.

Interest in Meet-Cute May Be Part of a Desire for More Authenticity and IRL Events

Seeking a meet-cute could help people meet what's apparently a growing, widespread desire for more authenticity and IRL events, in general. Such a desire may represent a backlash against the rise of online dating and so many other online things like social media that make it difficult to tell what's ultimately real as opposed to carefully manicured and fake. Plus, the loneliness epidemic, which has been incidentally spreading over the same period of time as the rise of online stuff, may be leaving more and more people seriously craving IRL connection.

How Should Meet-Cute Play a Role in Your Dating?

Of course, being able to tell others your meet-cute story doesn't have to be your primary goal in dating. It's OK if your initial meeting was as blah as buying a pair of straight-legged jeans online, as long as the relationship ends up being a good fit for both of you.

At the same time, this interest in meet-cutes is a reminder that even with the advent of online dating, many couples—in fact, probably the vast majority of couples—still meet the old-fashioned way initially. That is, IRL, in all sorts of ways—often unusual, unexpected, and seemingly chance. So don't feel that your only options are to use dating apps or professional matchmakers.

Instead, remain open to all sorts of possibilities. That includes doing things that you normally would find fun regardless of whether you find a date. You never know what might happen when you are enjoying yourself and thus potentially making yourself appear more attractive in the process. Some of the best things in life arise purely out of serendipity.

item.title: Why Do We Hurt the People We Love Most?
item.description:
Relationships

Why Do We Hurt the People We Love Most?

On why love requires taking the bitter with the sweet.

Posted October 3, 2026

Key points
  • The people who matter most can hurt us most precisely because they matter so much.
  • Intimacy requires honesty and mutual growth, not merely pleasant interactions.
  • The goal of love is not to eliminate all hurt, but to repair it and learn from it.

"You always hurt the one you love, the one you should not hurt at all…
So if I broke your heart last night, it's because I love you most of all." —The Mills Brothers

Love is among life's greatest rewards. Yet if love is rooted in care, why are we often kinder to strangers than to the people we love most? The answer lies in the paradox of intimacy: The closer someone is to us, the greater our capacity both to enrich their life and to hurt them. This paradox also explains why we sometimes treat strangers more kindly than our romantic partners.

Source: Gustavo Fring/Pexels

The Paradox of Romantic Intimacy

"Love of my life, you hurt me, you've broken my heart and now you leave me." —Queen

"My spouse said that if I (sexually) go elsewhere, he does not want to know about it." —A married woman

Intimacy is among the most valuable aspects of romantic relationships. It brings partners closer and makes their connection unique. However, as two lives become increasingly intertwined, opportunities for hurt also multiply. Lovers spend much of their lives together, and their decisions often have significant consequences for one another. Thus, dedication to one's work may leave a partner feeling neglected; an activity that delights one person may burden the other.

Profound intimacy, openness, and trust reduce the need for constant self-monitoring. Lovers are typically less guarded with each other than with strangers, and hasty remarks or impulsive actions can easily cause hurt. The freedom to be authentic comes with a cost: greater vulnerability. This challenges a widespread assumption that genuine love should protect us from hurt. Often, the opposite is true. The more important someone becomes in our lives, the greater their power to affect us, for better and for worse. Intimacy expands both our opportunities for fulfillment and our vulnerability to hurt.

Why We Are Kinder to Strangers

We are often more polite and forgiving toward strangers' minor shortcomings than toward those of our romantic partners. With partners, we may be more demanding, impatient, and occasionally hurtful. This pattern relates to several characteristics of romantic relationships: psychological closeness, deeply shared lives, and profound mutual concern.

Distance: The Double-Edged Nature of Closeness

A central difference between a romantic partner and a stranger is psychological distance. Our partners are deeply woven into our lives, whereas strangers usually have little influence on our well-being. Because a partner matters so much, their actions affect us more strongly. Closeness enriches our lives, but also creates vulnerability. Possessiveness, jealousy, insecurity, dependency, and fears of losing freedom often arise precisely because the relationship matters so much. A stranger's successes and failures barely affect us, whereas a partner's achievements, disappointments, and choices can significantly influence our own well-being. Accordingly, we react more intensely to a partner's shortcomings than to those of a stranger. The closeness that gives love its meaning can also make our responses harsher.

Shared Lives: Nurturing Caring Rather Than Mere Politeness

"Politeness is half good manners and half good lying." —Mary Wilson Little

Mutual nurturing is central to romantic love. Each partner's flourishing becomes intertwined with the other's, making their behavior highly significant. We take a partner's mistakes more seriously because their actions affect our shared life. Interactions with strangers, by contrast, are often guided by conventions of politeness.

Politeness smooths social encounters by softening criticism, overlooking minor offenses, and avoiding unnecessary conflicts. Such behavior is particularly important with strangers, who know little about us and can easily misunderstand us. Romantic relationships operate differently. Partners need kindness and tact, but genuine intimacy also requires honesty, which is not always pleasant. Telling a partner what troubles us may create temporary discomfort, yet it can strengthen the relationship and foster personal growth. Romantic love may involve less politeness but deeper concern. What appears unkind in the moment may sometimes express a deeper commitment to the relationship. Indeed, the opposite of love is not hurt but indifference. Hurt is often the price of caring deeply enough to become vulnerable.

Caring Calmness Versus Indifference

"Along with the sunshine, there's gotta be a little rain sometime." —Lynn Anderson

Calmness is often confused with indifference, but the two are different. Indifference reflects a lack of concern, whereas calmness can coexist with profound caring. In healthy relationships, calmness often emerges from security: We care deeply about the other person without reacting anxiously to every difficulty (Ben-Ze'ev, 2019).

A stranger's wrongdoing may leave us relatively unmoved because it has little relevance to us. A partner's behavior is different—we criticize and react because the relationship matters. In the short term, this may make us appear less kind to our partners than to strangers. Over time, however, we devote far more attention and effort to our partner's flourishing than we would ever devote to a stranger. Accordingly, greater criticism can coexist with greater caring. What matters is not how pleasant our behavior appears at a particular moment, but the broader context of commitment and concern.

Concluding Thoughts

"You've got to take the bitter with the sweet." —Carole King

Romantic life is a package deal. The same intimacy that brings joy, meaning, and fulfillment also exposes us to disappointment, frustration, and heartache. We can reduce the risk of being hurt by maintaining emotional distance, but doing so may deprive us of some of life's richest experiences. Strangers make relatively few claims on our lives, allowing us to remain polite and detached. Love is different. It demands vulnerability, forgiveness, patience, honesty, and the ability to repair inevitable wounds.

Hurting the beloved is therefore not always a sign of insufficient love. Often, it is a by-product of profound intimacy. The deeper our investment in a relationship, the greater our vulnerability, expectations, and potential for conflict. The truest measure of caring is not momentary politeness but enduring commitment. Meaningful love does not offer only sweetness. Its unique rewards require a willingness to accept both the bitter and the sweet (Wong & Mayer, 2023).

The central question is not whether we will hurt those we love, but rather whether love is resilient enough to absorb and repair these injuries. Relationships flourish not when partners never hurt one another, but when they learn to transform inevitable wounds into deeper understanding. The Mills Brothers' lyric is wrong in one respect: Hurting the one we love is not proof that we love them most; rather, it reflects the fact that love makes us vulnerable enough to matter deeply to one another.

item.title: Why Do I Shut Down During Conflict?
item.description:
Relationships

Why Do I Shut Down During Conflict?

Going numb can protect us. It can also pull us away from the people we love.

Posted October 3, 2026

Key points
  • Shutting down in conflict can be protective, not a sign that you don't care.
  • Conflict can activate old stories about harm, fairness, safety, or whether it's worth staying engaged.
  • The hard part is noticing when protection starts pulling you out of the relationship.

Apologies in advance to my husband for revealing this terrible secret, but: we argue. And sometimes when we argue, there’s this moment when things just go numb. I can picture it—one second things are red hot, my chest is tight, voices are raised, and I’m making my case, trying to get him to understand me. And then the next moment: nothing. It’s not like I get calm or sad or even resigned. It’s the total absence of feeling. It’s like all the energy I had for this fight (whether it was actually doing any good or not) just teleported to another dimension. I can feel my husband’s frustration in moments like these. He sees me go from engaged to disengaged in a split second. He wants to keep talking, but I’m already gone.

And let me be clear: Shutting down doesn’t feel like a choice in that moment. It’s not a powerful tool that I’ve devised to send all my negative emotions to some cosmic emotional landfill. Like so many of the strategies we learn, numbing out in moments of conflict is a way for me to protect myself. Our nervous system has a whole repertoire of responses to threat (fighting, running away, freezing, shutting down) that developed for good reasons. But sometimes the threat we’re responding to right now is not a predator threatening our lives; it’s our loved one telling us they’re hurting.

You may find yourself thinking—but that doesn’t make sense. If I love this person, why would I be triggered by their pain? I wish it were that simple. But sometimes something happens in the present that bears more than a passing resemblance to a story that we’ve been carrying for a long time. And once this story joins the party, the argument is no longer about whatever started it; something older is here too.

When it stops being about the argument

I’ve always been scared that my anger will hurt the people I love. It’s a story I’ve carried with me since I was little. I know where it comes from, and I’ve had a lifetime of experience that seems to confirm it. And so when I see the pain unfolding in front of me, even though logically I know that it’s not my pain to own, I shut down. That story says, “You have to stop, you monster. You’re harming him.” I also hold a story that says the deck is stacked against me. Some part of me is always calculating the odds and assessing the rules to see if I have a fair shot. And when that part decides things are unfair, it would rather I walk away than keep trying. I think it’s afraid it will hurt too much to try and fail. We all have our own versions of these—stories that come online and convince us that we can’t stay with what is currently happening.

But that disconnection just leads to more disconnection. My shutting down doesn’t actually stop my husband from feeling pain. It just creates distance. I see the pain in his eyes when I close off, the missed opportunity to work through something together even though it is hard because we’re worth it. But his disappointment just deepens my own commitment to the story. Some part of me is trying to protect me and my relationships, and instead is actually harming them. If you see yourself in this pattern, I hope you can find some compassion for how impossible it can feel.

The space for two

It’s incredibly difficult to stay connected to your experience while also making room for the experience of someone you love. In therapy-speak, we call this differentiation. At its core, differentiation is the ability to stay connected to another person without losing your own connection to yourself. Differentiation lets us see that our partner disagreeing with us doesn’t necessarily mean that the rules are unfair. Differentiation gives us the space to see that the pain of our partner doesn’t necessarily mean that we’re a monster. Differentiation allows a couple to have their own hobbies and still make time to build LEGO together. That last one was me and my husband. But let’s be honest—they’re all me and my husband.

Differentiation doesn’t mean agreeing, and it doesn’t mean staying in a conversation that has become unhealthy or unproductive. It doesn’t mean burying your feelings so your partner can feel theirs. It does mean creating enough space so both of you and your feelings and your needs can co-exist in the same conversation.

Finding more choice

As I try to untangle my habit of shutting down, I find myself less interested in stopping it from happening and more curious about what I might be able to do instead. Maybe I could share that I’m feeling overwhelmed. Maybe I need to ask for a time-out and be clear about when I’m coming back. But I know that I can’t argue these stories out of existence, and honestly, as I get older, I’m less interested in trying. I’m going to get triggered. I’m human. But I do want to have more choice about what I do when it happens.

The stories inside me want me to believe that if I shut down, the conflict disappears too. But that’s just not true. My husband is still there. Our marriage is still there. I’m still there too. I’m grateful that shutting down helped me stay safe at one time or another, but I’m not interested in letting it distance me from the people I love. We’ve got lots of LEGO to build. And so I get curious: What happens to the conversation if I stay?

item.title: Your 80-Year-Old Self Has Wisdom You Need Today
item.description:
Relationships

Your 80-Year-Old Self Has Wisdom You Need Today

Research on aging can help you make better decisions when you’re feeling stuck.

Posted October 3, 2026

Key points
  • Long-term regret comes from inaction, not mistakes.
  • Relationships are the most important predictor of health and happiness.
  • Imagining your future self improves today's decisions.

Big decisions can feel paralyzing. Starting a business. Changing jobs. Prioritizing your time. How do you make the best choices now when you’re not sure how things will work out? What if you had the wisdom of your 80-year-old self right now to help you make better decisions?

Research suggests you might have it, but not realize it.

Research on Regret Reveals What Matters Most

Classic research on feeling regret shows that it changes over the course of life. Most of us think that the things we regret most are our mistakes. That’s not true as we age.

There are two types of regret. Short-term regret involves things you did that you wish you didn’t. Like giving a poorly worded response in an important business meeting. Or saying something hurtful to your spouse.

As we age, our sense of regret shifts. Regret tied to the things we did stop mattering as much. Instead, we start feeling regret about the things we didn’t do. The job opportunities we passed up. The conversations we avoided. The travel we never did. Or the risks we decided not to take.

At 80, it’s much more likely you’ll stop asking yourself “Why did I?” and instead think “Why didn’t I?” That means if you consulted your 80-year-old self right now, you might get advice to do something adventurous, courageous, or just plain fun.

Time Changes What You Value

When people believe they have unlimited time ahead of them, they tend to focus “outward.” Achievements like job promotions, awards, or professional accolades feel most important.

However, when you feel like time is limited, maybe because of an illness or just being older, your priorities shift. More emotionally meaningful experiences like volunteering, doing things that give you a sense of satisfaction, and deepening relationships become center stage.

For example, in one study, young people who were asked to imagine their remaining time as limited immediately shifted their priorities. At 80, you’ll likely realize you want to spend more time with the people you care about, do the things that feel the most meaningful to you, and maximize every moment you have left.

Research Says Relationships Make You Healthy

The Harvard Study of Adult Development has followed participants for more than 85 years. It tracks health, careers, relationships, and life satisfaction and is the longest-running study of adult well-being in history. Researchers examined what best predicted health and happiness. The strongest single predictor? The quality of your relationships.

In my leadership development programs, I often ask executives to reflect on what gives their work genuine meaning. The conversations go deep and consistently reveal the same gap. Most people spend most of their time working. What they actually care about most gets the least amount of time. Like their closest relationships, mostly with family and friends.

People generally know that their relationships matter most. But the pressures of daily life get in the way of prioritizing time for them, and that can harm both their physical health and emotional well-being.

Consult Your Future Self

Taken together, the research points to a practical tool: borrow perspective from the self you'll eventually become.

You can't know exactly what your 80-year-old self will think. But decades of data on regret, time perception, and lasting fulfillment provide solid clues.

The next time you face an important decision, sit with these questions:

  • What opportunity am I passing up?
  • Which relationships am I underinvesting in right now?
  • Where am I spending significant time that won't matter 20 years from now?

When you consider these questions, you’re using proven research to expand your focus and see what really matters. The research shows you already have the wisdom of your 80-year-old self. Use it to make better decisions today.

item.title: Your AI Therapist Will See You Now
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Your AI Therapist Will See You Now

Can a chatbot do what your (human) therapist does?

Posted October 3, 2026

Key points
  • In some ways, AI therapy can be comparable to human therapists.
  • AI therapy bots’ are more effective in the short-term and less so in the long-term.
  • There is plenty of interventions that AI therapy bots cannot do.

The whiplash around AI these days is real: One minute, we’re hearing from the most powerful AI leaders of our time that the technology could arguably kill us all. A minute later, we’re seeing an ad for the latest AI therapy-bot or app appear in our algorithm, offering a cheaper, more convenient alternative to human therapists.

All this is happening within the larger geopolitical and environmental context of the debate surrounding AI data centers and the enormous ecological cost of running these systems. This begs the question: Can you, or should you, consider an AI therapist?

Human Versus AI Throwdown: Therapy Edition

If we momentarily put aside carbon footprint concerns, recent research directly comparing the effectiveness of AI versus human mental health professionals is telling. When researchers showed therapists transcripts of conversations between patients and 1) an AI therapy bot and 2) a human therapist, the professionals couldn’t reliably tell the difference between the two. Their performance hovered around chance (53 percent accuracy). What’s more, the transcripts with the AI therapists scored higher on quality.

AI therapists and human ones can be surprisingly hard to tell apart
Source: Pavel Danilyuk/Pexels

Another study went a step further, reviewing well over a dozen randomized controlled trials involving thousands of participants to test the relative efficacy of AI therapy versus no therapy or more traditional forms, including treatment-as-usual with humans and other types of interventions (like self-help books). They found that in the short term, AI therapy did improve outcomes for both depression and anxiety, but the benefits didn’t seem to last past the three-month mark.

Neither of these directly and consistently pitted AI bots against real flesh-and-blood therapists. The jury is clearly still out when it comes to that throwdown.

Perks and Liabilities of AI Therapy

Still, if you’re wondering how a chatbot could compare to a human in alleviating mental health issues, these researchers point out that an AI therapist is available at all hours and offers immediate care, which may be a reason for their effectiveness in these studies. Moreover, most of these chatbots studied relied on Cognitive Behavioral Therapy techniques, which have long been established as interventions for depressive and anxiety symptoms.

There are plenty of highly effective interventions AI bots arguably can’t do, at least not in their current iterations, like providing exposure therapy (for phobias) or prescribing medication. It’s also possible that the placebo effect could be driving at least some of the current findings. If people expect AI therapy to work, it may end up doing so.

All this is to say: human therapists are still as important as ever. AI therapy can help if you need an immediate, short-term dose of CBT, but its benefits may likely taper out over time. The question, then, may not be either-or, but yes, and?

item.title: Are Parentification and Eating Disorders Connected?
item.description:
Parentification

Are Parentification and Eating Disorders Connected?

Early role reversal has long-term mental health effects.

Posted October 3, 2026

Key points
  • Eating disorders are one potential mental health condition that can emerge from childhood parentification.
  • Insecure attachment may be one attachment type commonly seen in parentification and eating disorders.
  • By learning how parentification and eating disorders overlap, clinicians can better identify and treat both.

As someone who talks about parentification (a lot), I’ve come to recognize that the connection between eating disorders and parent-child role reversal may not be explicitly clear. There is a winding road among different psychopathologies that may develop as a result of parentification, and eating-disordered behavior is but one of many potential stops on that path. For example, children who experience parentification may become adults who experience depression, anxiety, and alcohol use disorder. Despite this, researchers have found that the impact of parentification on eating disorders, personality disorders, and anxiety disorders is greater than on mood disorders and alcohol use disorder (Hooper and colleagues, 2011). Can we better understand such a complex interplay?

The Importance of Early Attachment Relationships

To grow up with a sense that the world is a safe place, children need to develop healthy attachment relationships with their caregivers. We can understand attachment as the process of bonding with your caregiver as an infant and young child. If you grow up with nurturing, responsive caregivers, your attachment style tends to develop securely and healthily. However, if you grow up with caregivers who are emotionally unavailable, distant, anxious, or absent, your attachment style tends to develop in a more insecure way, causing relational problems later in adulthood.

The Impact of Disruptions in the Attachment Relationship

Parentification acts as a form of attachment disruption. For example, parents who place unrealistic pressure on children to perform adult tasks, either emotionally or logistically, are often unavailable or inconsistent. They look to their children to fill their own emotional needs; this is pressure on a child with little power to do so. Additionally, when children cannot rely on a parent for support, they feel completely on their own. This builds an overwhelming sense of responsibility and makes it difficult for them to ask for help later in life. When help is inconsistent or non-existent, the child often stops looking for it.

There is evidence that suggests attachment disruptions, particularly those that influence the development of insecure attachment, play a part in eating disorders and related mental health distress (Attili and colleagues, 2018). Researchers have also found that the link between attachment and eating disorders is mediated by other factors including emotional dysregulation, depressive symptoms, body dissatisfaction, and perfectionism (Cortés-García and colleagues, 2019).

Potential Overlap Between Eating Disorders and Parentification

Many people, including professionals, have little knowledge of treating eating disorders (Johns and colleagues, 2019). Myths abound, and incorrect assumptions can prevent an accurate understanding of eating disorders from emerging. The “9 Truths About Eating Disorders” (Bulik, 2015) cuts through popular assumptions and provides a useful guide to help us understand eating disorders. Here are a few of the truths about eating disorders from Bulik’s list, along with my analysis of how parentification, if present, could connect.

1) Many people with eating disorders look healthy yet may be extremely ill.

Parentified children are often fearful about taking up space, adding to a parent’s burden, or failing at just about everything. Compulsive exercise, restricted food or fluid intake, or obsessiveness over body image may emerge as means of coping with an environment in which there is little children can control or feel safe in.

2) An eating disorder diagnosis is a health crisis that disrupts personal and family functioning.

Eating disorders may emerge as an attempt to maintain stability in unstable inner and outer environments. Because people may ‘look’ healthy on the surface and may go to great lengths to conceal their eating struggles or disorder, it can be easy to overlook the severity until families notice more glaring symptoms—if ever. Parentified children typically try to stay under the radar and are very good at masking their pain in front of family and friends—as a means of survival.

3) Genes and environment play important roles in the development of eating disorders.

Though the role of nature versus nurture has been painted as a debate, we can understand mental distress as a mix of both the genetic blueprint that we’re born with and what we experience in our environments growing up. Certain genetic and environmental conditions exist that make it more likely that parentification will occur, including the mental health issues of one or both parents, parental substance use, single parenthood, the death of one parent, and how parents themselves deal with stress.

Noticing and being aware of the overlap between parentification and eating disorders can help clinicians be mindful that if one condition is present, it’s good practice to take a closer look and see if the other could benefit from care and attention as well.

Source: Peoplecreations vs Magnific

item.title: How Culture Shapes Language and Shapes Us
item.description:
Cross-Cultural Psychology

How Culture Shapes Language and Shapes Us

Muhammad Ali's poem and the influence of pronouns on our psychology.

Posted October 3, 2026

Key points
  • Language is encoded with cultural information that shapes thought and behavior.
  • Cross-cultural experimental studies suggest that priming people with different pronouns can influence them.
  • Findings are not uniform and priming research is often critiqued.
  • Consciously shifting the language we use could influence us beyond short-lived experimental effects.
Source: Clay Banks/Unsplash

In Spike Lee’s documentary covering the famed Rumble in the Jungle, Pulitzer Prize-winning writer Norman Mailer recalls one of the many memorable moments from the life of Muhammad Ali. Speaking to a group of students at Harvard, a spontaneous call from the crowd invites Ali to “give us a poem.” Mailer recalls that Ali pauses for a moment before pronouncing, “Me, we.” Mailer, the gifted wordsmith, fawns over Ali’s understated eloquence and suggests this is the shortest poem in the English language.

Ali was a dynamic figure: quintessentially American in his rags-to-riches, self-made success, yet global in stature and political dissent. This dynamism is embodied in his turn of phrase, which collapses the individualist approach into a collectivist one.

Collectivism and individualism are much discussed within the field. According to the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis, languages encode distinct cultural cognitions that encourage speakers of the language to adopt specific cultural perspectives.

Intra- and Intercultural Differences

Across three experiments, Na and Choi (2009) showed that collectivist Koreans were more likely to rely on wuri, which is equivalent to “our,” than nae, which is equivalent to “my,” when translating compared to compatriots who scored highly on individualism. When Americans and Koreans were exposed to a third language, Wezwe (spoken in New Guinea), Koreans relied significantly more on first-person plural pronouns than Americans.

Shifting Trends

Yu and colleagues analyzed first-person pronouns in nine languages using Google Ngram, spanning 59 years (2016). What they found was fascinating. Eight of the nine languages saw an increased use of first-person singular pronouns, which the authors argue is evidence for a rise in individualism. Interestingly, the only language where this trend was not reported was British English. The authors suggest this might be due to the use of British English among people of collectivist cultures (South Asia and Southeast Asia), or due to a diversification of meaning for words like we. The others included Chinese, American English, Hebrew, Italian, and Russian, and a clear increase in the use of first-person singular pronouns was reported: “We can conclude that a majority of the cultures we examined became more individualistic over time,” the authors note in their conclusion.

Source: DJ Paine/Unsplash

Shifting Your Thoughts and Behavior?

Experimental researchers have reported on ways to change decision-making and behavior based on pronouns used.

Mishra and Bost Jr. used a priming task involving first-person singular pronouns (I/me/my) or first-person plural pronouns (we/us/our) and found that priming significantly affected the weighting of different performance behaviors when assessing others’ job performance (2018). Specifically, those primed with the plural pronouns and collectivist mindset rated citizenship behaviors as more significant and relevant when assessing overall performance. They also found that the collectivist priming correlated with lower weighting of counterproductive workplace behaviors; the authors suggest this might reflect a collectivist tendency to be less forthcoming with criticism. This explanation can be challenged by suggesting that collectivist mindsets will be concerned with group performance.

Jiao and Zhao relied on a dictator game; the participant decides several payoffs for themselves and another person to investigate individualist-collectivist priming (2023). They also used a pronoun-circling exercise used by Mishra and Bost Jr., adding a task in which participants were asked to imagine and describe two scenarios: one with an individual tennis player playing a final match, and the other with a tennis team doing something similar. They reported that participants primed toward collectivism proposed a higher offer on average, which participants were also more likely to accept.

Results have not always been uniform, though. He and colleagues used a social-value orientation task by Murphy and colleagues, another dictator game, to assess prosocial behavior among a group of participants (2020, 2011). Prosociality is assessed by how fair the payoffs are. Participants were manipulated by reading one of two sets of instructions. The “with-I” condition’s instructions were laden with the first-person pronoun “I” (I will receive $100; I will decide how to split it). The second set of instructions were written without the first-person pronoun (Receive $100_). Counterintuitively, participants primed with the “I” condition generally made more prosocial decisions.

Conclusion

This lack of uniformity speaks to challenges to priming efficacy in general. In my own study that relied on framing to effect change, we found a stark difference between the strength of moral foundations in predicting prosocial behavior and that of our framing effect. In short, moral foundations themselves were robustly predictive while experimental manipulations were fleeting. Embodying prosocial attitudes and behaviors is likely about more than being primed or framed into things and behaving differently, with our use of language as one potential starting point to affect change. The language we use runs deeper than a prime and is encoded with meaning and assumptions; training ourselves to adjust it could be a powerful means to change how we think about the world. This is the wisdom that Ali seemed to capture in just two words.
